title: The Machine
subtitle: How American kidney care actually works: the 1972 promise, the money, the consolidation, and the gaps people fall through
outcomes: Explain why kidney failure is the only disease with its own Medicare entitlement, and what that payment design rewards
Trace where the money flows in a dialysis treatment, and why a commercially insured patient is worth several times a Medicare patient
Describe how two companies came to operate about three-quarters of U.S. dialysis facilities, and what enforcement records show
Map the hand-offs where patients fall through a fragmented system, from late diagnosis to missing transplant referrals
Read the outcome data the system produces and connect each number to a design choice

scenes.text: Welcome. I'm Avery, and for the next forty-five minutes I'm going to take you inside a machine most people only ever see from the chair. Not the dialysis machine. The system around it. How it is paid for, who owns it, who decides, and why so many people are carried along by it instead of being served by it.

v.sub: Why kidney failure has its own Medicare program, and what that design rewards

scenes.text: This course is self-paced. You can pause me, rewind, or read along with the captions. Every number I give you has a source, and you can open it from the sources panel. When I describe a lawsuit or a settlement, I will tell you exactly what was proven and what was only alleged. An advocate who gets the facts wrong hands the other side a gift.

v.title: How this course works
items: Self-paced: pause, rewind, read the captions
Every figure is sourced: open the Sources panel any time
Short checks after each module; a final assessment at the end

scenes.text: Start in 1972. That year, Congress amended the Social Security Act so that almost anyone with kidney failure could get Medicare, no matter their age. Coverage began in July 1973. It remains the only time Medicare has been opened to people because of one specific diagnosis. It was a genuine act of mercy. Before it, hospital committees literally decided who would get a dialysis machine and who would die.

items.t: Scarce dialysis machines; hospital committees choose who is treated
Social Security Amendments extend Medicare to people with kidney failure
Coverage begins
Still the only diagnosis-specific Medicare entitlement

scenes.text: But notice what the promise paid for. It paid for treatment once the kidneys had already failed. It did not pay anyone to find kidney disease early, to slow it down, or to get someone a transplant before they needed dialysis. A payment system is a set of instructions. This one said: we will pay, generously and reliably, at the end.

v.text: A payment system is a set of instructions. The 1972 design paid reliably for the end stage, and almost nothing for keeping people from reaching it.

scenes.text: Here is the scale today. More than eight hundred and eight thousand people in the United States are living with kidney failure. About two thirds of them are on dialysis. About one third live with a transplant. In 2021, Medicare spent fifty-two point three billion dollars on kidney failure alone.

v.src: NIDDK, citing USRDS 2023 Annual Data Report

scenes.text: And behind that group stands a much larger one. About fourteen percent of American adults, roughly thirty-seven million people, have chronic kidney disease. Before I give you the next number, I want you to guess it. Of those thirty-seven million, what share do you think know they have it?

v.label: U.S. adults with chronic kidney disease (about 14%)
v.src: CDC, Chronic Kidney Disease in the United States, NHANES 2021–2023

scenes.prompt: Of the roughly 37 million U.S. adults with chronic kidney disease, what percent are UNAWARE they have it?
scenes.fb: About 87% of adults with CKD do not know they have it (CDC, NHANES 2021–2023). The disease is usually silent until the late stages, and routine testing is not built into how primary care is paid.

scenes.text: Eighty-seven percent. Nearly nine in ten people with a disease that can end in dialysis do not know they have it. That is not a personal failing. It is the predictable result of a system that pays for the end of the road and very little for the road itself. Keep that idea with you. Almost everything in this course traces back to it.

v.label: 87 of every 100 adults with CKD don't know they have it

scenes.text: In the next module we'll follow one person through the years before dialysis, and find the exact points where the system could have caught them, and didn't.

quiz.q: What made the 1972 Social Security Amendments unique in Medicare's history?
o: They extended Medicare to people because of one specific diagnosis, kidney failure, regardless of age
They required dialysis companies to be nonprofit
They created the organ transplant waiting list
quiz.why: Kidney failure remains the only diagnosis that opens Medicare to people of any age. Coverage began in July 1973.

quiz.q: About what share of U.S. adults with chronic kidney disease are unaware they have it?
quiz.why: CDC estimates about 87% of adults with CKD do not know it (NHANES 2021–2023).

quiz.q: What did the original payment design reliably reward?
o: Treatment after the kidneys had already failed
quiz.why: The entitlement paid for end-stage treatment, not for finding and slowing the disease earlier.

sources.t: CDC: Chronic Kidney Disease in the United States, 2023
NIDDK: Kidney Disease Statistics for the United States (USRDS 2023)

scenes.text: Imagine a woman in her fifties. Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, a busy job. She sees her primary care doctor once a year. Her kidneys have been losing function for a decade. Nobody has told her, because nobody ordered the two simple tests that would have shown it: a blood test for filtration, and a urine test for protein.

She is not unusual. About thirty-eight percent of adults with diabetes have chronic kidney disease. About twenty-one percent of adults with high blood pressure do. These are the two largest roads into kidney failure, and the people on them are already in front of a doctor. The failure is not access to a clinic. It is what happens, or doesn't happen, once they are there.

Now follow her forward. Kidney specialists, nephrologists, are supposed to be involved long before dialysis, to slow the disease, plan the safest way to dialyze, and refer for transplant. In the national data, only about a third of people starting dialysis had seen a nephrologist at least a year before. About one in five had no record of nephrology care at all before their kidneys failed.

v.title: Nephrology care before starting dialysis
v.src: Han & Saran, Kidney360 2020, citing USRDS (2017 data)

scenes.text: That timing shows up in her arm, or in her chest. The safest way to do hemodialysis is through a fistula, a connection a surgeon builds in the arm months in advance. The riskiest is a catheter, a tube in a large vein near the heart, with a high risk of infection and death. In the same national data, about eighty percent of people started hemodialysis through a catheter. Only seventeen percent started with a fistula.

items: Built by a surgeon in the arm

b.tag: What a crash start looks like

scenes.text: And the gap is directly tied to care. Among people who had more than a year of nephrology care, about half still started on a catheter. Among people with no nephrology care, ninety-three percent did. Late arrival is not bad luck. It is a measurable product of a missed referral.

Clinicians have a name for what happened to our patient. A crash start. She walks into an emergency room short of breath and swollen, and leaves days later with a catheter in her chest and a dialysis schedule. Her first months on dialysis will be the most dangerous of her life. Every decision about her future, home dialysis, transplant, where she dialyzes, will now be made in a hurry, by someone else.

v.title: Where the system could have caught her
v.note: Each red step is a hand-off that commonly does not happen.

scenes.prompt: You're helping our patient at her annual visit. Her filtration rate has been falling for three years. Which request does the most to change her future?

options.t: Ask the doctor to keep watching it next year
options.fb: Watching is exactly how a decade passes. Falling function is a reason to act now, not to wait.

options.t: Ask for a urine albumin test, a nephrology referral, and a written plan for slowing the decline
options.fb: Right. The urine test catches damage the blood test misses, the referral brings in a specialist years earlier, and a written plan creates accountability.
Too early and aimed at the wrong goal. The aim right now is to slow the disease and plan ahead, including transplant.

scenes.text: Here is a fact many patients never hear. In the United States, a person can be added to the kidney transplant waiting list and start earning waiting time once their filtration rate falls to twenty or below, before ever starting dialysis. A transplant before dialysis, called preemptive, generally produces the best outcomes. But it only happens if someone starts the referral early enough.

v.text: Waiting time for a deceased-donor kidney can start at a filtration rate of 20 or below, before dialysis. A late referral can cost a patient years on the list.

scenes.text: So here is your first advocate's tool. When kidney function is falling, ask three questions, in writing if you have to. Have you tested my urine for protein? When will I see a nephrologist? And when can I be referred for a transplant evaluation? Those three questions close most of the gap you just saw.

v.title: Three questions that close the gap
items: Have you tested my urine for albumin (protein)?
When will I see a nephrologist?
When can I be referred for a transplant evaluation?

quiz.q: In the national data cited, about what share of people started hemodialysis through a catheter?
quiz.why: About 80% started through a catheter; only 17% through a fistula (USRDS 2017 data, via Kidney360).

quiz.q: Among people with NO nephrology care before kidney failure, what share started on a catheter?
quiz.why: 93% with no prior nephrology care, versus 52% with more than a year of it.

quiz.q: When can a person begin accruing waiting time for a deceased-donor kidney?
o: Only after a year on dialysis
When filtration rate is 20 or below, or once dialysis starts
Only after a transplant center visit
quiz.why: Waiting time can begin at an eGFR of 20 or below, even before dialysis, which is why early referral matters.

quiz.q: Which test catches kidney damage that a filtration blood test can miss?
quiz.why: Urine albumin shows kidney damage even when filtration still looks acceptable.

sources.t: CDC: Chronic Kidney Disease in the United States
Han & Saran, Global Dialysis Perspective: United States, Kidney360 (2020)
OPTN: Kidney waiting time policy

scenes.text: If you want to understand any system, follow the money. In dialysis, the money moves in a pattern that explains decisions patients often find baffling, from why they're pushed toward certain insurance to why a clinic opens in one neighborhood and not another.

v.sub: Why one patient can be worth four times another

scenes.text: Medicare pays dialysis facilities a fixed, bundled amount per treatment, updated every year. The bundle covers the treatment and most related drugs and labs. On its own, that sounds orderly. What matters is how it compares with what private insurance pays for the very same treatment.

v.text: Medicare pays one bundled rate per treatment. Private insurers negotiate their own rates, and they are far higher.

scenes.text: A 2019 analysis in JAMA Internal Medicine looked at the largest provider's own disclosures. In 2017, commercial insurance paid that company an average of one thousand and forty-one dollars per treatment. Government insurance paid two hundred and forty-eight. Over a year of treatments, that is about a hundred and forty-nine thousand dollars for one privately insured patient, against about thirty-five thousand for a Medicare or Medicaid patient.

v.title: Average payment per treatment, 2017
v.src: JAMA Internal Medicine (2019), as reported by Undark (2020)

scenes.text: The most recent federal data tells the same story. In its March 2026 report to Congress, the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission noted one large dialysis organization reported that commercially insured patients were eleven percent of its U.S. patients, but about thirty-three percent of its U.S. dialysis revenue in 2024.

v.src: MedPAC, March 2026 Report to the Congress, Ch. 5

scenes.text: Look at Medicare's side of the ledger too. In 2024, traditional Medicare spent seven point six billion dollars on outpatient dialysis for about two hundred and forty thousand beneficiaries. The Commission estimated freestanding facilities earned a four and a half percent margin on Medicare patients that year, after a slightly negative margin the year before. In other words, Medicare roughly covers costs. The profit is made elsewhere.

v.src: MedPAC, March 2026 Report to the Congress, Ch. 5

scenes.text: Now add one rule. When someone with job-based insurance develops kidney failure, that private plan must stay the primary payer for a thirty-month coordination period before Medicare takes over. Those thirty months are, financially, the most valuable months of a patient's treatment. Everything about how patients are counseled on insurance should be read with that in mind.

items.t: Kidney failure; employer plan is primary payer
Private plan pays commercial rates
Medicare becomes primary at the bundled rate

scenes.text: In 2022 the Supreme Court decided a case about those months. An employer health plan had treated outpatient dialysis as out-of-network and paid low rates. The largest dialysis company sued, arguing the plan was illegally pushing kidney patients toward Medicare. The Court ruled seven to two for the plan, because its limits applied to everyone equally. Bills called the Restore Protections for Dialysis Patients Act were introduced in response.

v.h: Marietta Memorial Hospital Employee Health Benefit Plan v. DaVita Inc.
v.sub: U.S. Supreme Court, 2022 · decided 7–2 for the health plan
items: Plan paid low, out-of-network rates for outpatient dialysis
Court: no violation of the Medicare Secondary Payer law, because the terms applied to all members
Response: Restore Protections for Dialysis Patients Act (S. 4750 / H.R. 8594, 117th Congress)

scenes.text: There is one more channel. Many low-income dialysis patients get help paying private insurance premiums from a charity, the American Kidney Fund. Reporting based on company disclosures found that in 2018 the two largest dialysis companies gave the fund about two hundred and forty-seven million dollars, roughly eighty percent of its budget that year. Help paying premiums can be a lifeline. It can also keep a patient on the most profitable insurance.

v.label: reported 2018 donations from the two largest dialysis companies to the American Kidney Fund, about 80% of its budget
v.src: Undark (2020); the Fund's own filings do not name donors

scenes.text: California tried to address it. A 2019 state law, AB 290, would have paid Medicare-level rates for patients whose premiums were covered by such charities. A federal judge blocked it with a preliminary injunction before it took effect. The legal fight that followed is a lesson in how hard it is to change a business model through one state law.

items.t: Signed: Medicare-level rates for charity-assisted patients; disclosure of grantees
Federal judge grants preliminary injunction before it takes effect

scenes.prompt: Tap each card. Who benefits from each payment rule?

cards.b: Keeps private plans paying first. Valuable to providers; meant to stop employers from shifting costs to Medicare.
Can keep a low-income patient insured. Also keeps them on coverage that pays providers several times Medicare.
Predictable for Medicare. Means each treatment, not each healthy month, is the unit that gets paid.

scenes.text: None of this means a single person in a clinic is acting in bad faith. It means the incentives point in a direction, and systems tend to drift the way their incentives point. Your job as an advocate is to see the incentive first, and then ask whose interest a given recommendation serves.

v.text: Before you weigh a recommendation, ask: under the payment rules, who gains if I say yes?

quiz.q: In the 2017 data cited, about how much did commercial insurance pay the largest provider per treatment, compared with government insurance?
o: About four times as much ($1,041 vs $248)
quiz.why: Commercial paid an average of $1,041 per treatment versus $248 for government insurance (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2019).

quiz.why: The Court ruled 7–2 for the health plan because its terms applied equally to all members.

quiz.q: For how long must an employer plan remain primary payer after a member develops kidney failure?
quiz.why: The Medicare Secondary Payer coordination period is 30 months.

o: A federal judge blocked it with a preliminary injunction

scenes.text: There were seven thousand six hundred and five dialysis facilities in the United States in 2024. According to the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, the two largest dialysis organizations, Fresenius Medical Care and DaVita, operated about three quarters of them, and about three quarters of Medicare's fee-for-service treatments.

v.label: About 3 of every 4 U.S. dialysis facilities are operated by two companies

scenes.text: When two companies run three quarters of the chairs, competition looks different. In much of the country, a patient's realistic choice of clinic is between two locations of the same company, or between the two companies. Market power shapes prices with private insurers, staffing, and how much leverage any one patient has when something goes wrong.

v.text: Choice of clinic is the basic tool patients are told they have. In a market this concentrated, it is often a choice between two locations of the same company.

scenes.text: Consolidation was built partly through relationships with the doctors who decide where patients dialyze. In 2014, DaVita agreed to pay three hundred and fifty million dollars, plus a thirty-nine million dollar civil forfeiture, to resolve allegations that it used joint ventures with nephrologists to induce patient referrals. It did not admit liability. It also signed a corporate integrity agreement with an independent monitor.

items: Alleged: clinic interests sold to referring nephrologists on favorable terms to secure referrals (2005–2014)
Alleged: non-competes that kept physicians from advising patients about competing clinics
No admission of liability; Corporate Integrity Agreement with an independent monitor

scenes.text: It was not the last case. In 2015, DaVita agreed to pay four hundred and fifty million dollars to resolve allegations that it billed for drug waste it created by choosing larger vials. In July 2024, it agreed to pay more than thirty-four million dollars to resolve allegations of kickbacks involving its former pharmacy, physician-owned vascular access centers, and a nephrology practice. Again, no determination of liability.

v.title: Federal settlements, DaVita (allegations; no admission of liability)

items.t: $350M + $39M forfeiture: physician joint venture kickback allegations
$450M: alleged billing for avoidable drug waste
$34.5M: alleged kickbacks (pharmacy referrals, vascular access centers, nephrology practice)

v.src: U.S. Department of Justice press releases

scenes.text: The other giant has its own record. In 2012, Fresenius products called GranuFlo and NaturaLyte, used in the dialysis solution, were the subject of a Class One recall, the most serious kind. In 2016, the company agreed to a two hundred and fifty million dollar settlement of the lawsuits that followed.

items: Class I recall of dialysate products (2012)

scenes.text: Market power also shows up at the ballot box. California voters were asked three times, in 2018, 2020 and 2022, to tighten rules on dialysis clinics, from capping profits to requiring a doctor or nurse practitioner on site and public infection reporting. The measures were sponsored by a health care workers union. All three failed. Reporting found the industry spent upwards of a hundred and ten million dollars in 2018 alone. For 2022, both sides together raised at least ninety-four million, about eighty-five percent of it from DaVita and Fresenius.

v.title: California dialysis ballot fights
v.src: Undark (2020); KFF Health News / Los Angeles Times (2022)

scenes.text: Here's the point to hold on to. Enforcement settlements, recalls and ballot spending are public records. Most patients and care partners never see them assembled in one place. That is why the Cold Ischemia Foundation built the Watch List, which scores fifty companies on exactly this kind of public record every week.

v.text: Public records exist. The advantage goes to whoever bothers to assemble them. See the Watch List on this site.

scenes.prompt: A clinic tells your father he can't switch to a competitor's location across town. What's the most accurate response?

options.t: Accept it. The clinic decides where patients dialyze.
options.fb: Patients have the right to be informed and to participate in decisions about their care, including transfer. The clinic does not own the patient.

options.t: Ask the nephrologist and the receiving clinic directly whether they'll accept him, and request the transfer in writing
options.fb: Right. Transfers depend on a physician with privileges and a willing receiving facility. Asking in writing creates a record.
Escalation has an order. Start with a clear written request; you'll learn the full ladder in Course 3.

quiz.why: About three quarters of 7,605 facilities (MedPAC, March 2026).

quiz.why: $350M plus a $39M forfeiture over alleged joint-venture kickbacks; no admission of liability.

quiz.why: Each DOJ release states the claims were allegations only, with no determination of liability. Accuracy protects your credibility.

scenes.text: Ask a simple question. Who is responsible for a person with kidney failure? The honest answer is: many people, each for a slice, and no one for the whole. That is fragmentation, and it is where most of the harm in this system happens. Not in one dramatic failure, but in the gaps between hand-offs.

v.sub: Fragmentation, and the hand-offs where people fall

scenes.text: Count the players. A primary care doctor. A nephrologist. The dialysis facility and its medical director. A vascular access surgeon or center. A transplant center, maybe more than one. An insurer, and since December 2024 a majority of people on dialysis are in Medicare Advantage plans, which have their own networks and rules. A regional ESRD Network that handles grievances. And a state survey agency that inspects facilities.

v.title: Who touches one patient's care
v.src: MedPAC, March 2026: 55% of dialysis beneficiaries in Medicare Advantage, Dec. 2024

scenes.text: That Medicare Advantage shift is recent. Until 2021, most people with kidney failure could not join a Medicare Advantage plan. The 21st Century Cures Act changed that starting in 2021. Within four years, a majority of people on dialysis had moved into private Medicare plans, each with its own network of clinics, nephrologists and transplant centers. A plan's network can quietly decide which transplant center a patient is even allowed to be evaluated at.

items.t: Most people with kidney failure barred from enrolling in Medicare Advantage
21st Century Cures Act opens Medicare Advantage to them
55% of dialysis beneficiaries in Medicare Advantage

scenes.prompt: A patient in a Medicare Advantage plan wants to be evaluated at a transplant center 40 minutes away, but the plan says it's out of network. What's the best first move?

options.fb: Network rules can often be appealed or excepted, and patients can sometimes change plans at set times.

options.t: Ask the plan in writing for its in-network transplant centers and its process for an exception or appeal, and note the next enrollment period when coverage can change
options.fb: Right. Get the network and the appeal process in writing. Plan choice itself becomes an advocacy tool at enrollment time.

options.t: Pay out of pocket for the whole evaluation
options.fb: That may be enormously expensive and unnecessary before exploring the plan's exception process.

scenes.text: Every arrow between those boxes is a hand-off, and every hand-off can drop. The best measured example is referral for transplant. In a study of every dialysis facility in Georgia, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in 2015, the median facility referred only about one in four patients for transplant evaluation within a year of starting dialysis.

v.label: median share of patients referred for transplant evaluation within a year of starting dialysis (Georgia facilities)

scenes.text: And the range is the real story. Some facilities referred no one. Others referred three quarters of their patients. Same state, same rules, same disease. The single biggest predictor of whether you were even considered for a transplant was which building you happened to dialyze in. The facilities with the lowest rates were more likely to serve high-poverty neighborhoods and had more patients per social worker.

v.title: Transplant referral within one year, by facility

scenes.prompt: Put the hand-offs in the order they should happen for someone whose kidney function is falling.
items: Planned dialysis start or preemptive transplant
scenes.fb: In practice, transplant referral and fistula planning overlap. The point is that both should happen before the first dialysis treatment, not after.

scenes.text: Medicare has tried to pay its way out of fragmentation with a series of experiments. The Kidney Care Choices model began in 2022, paying nephrology practices and kidney care organizations to manage total cost and outcomes. The ESRD Treatment Choices model adjusted payments to encourage home dialysis and transplant waitlisting. And in July 2025, a mandatory six-year model called IOTA began paying selected transplant hospitals based on their transplant performance.

v.title: Medicare's experiments with paying for the whole patient

items.t: Comprehensive ESRD Care model
ESRD Treatment Choices: incentives for home dialysis and transplant
Kidney Care Choices: total-cost arrangements for kidney practices
IOTA: six-year mandatory transplant hospital model
IOTA changes: Medicare Advantage patients included; waitlist status notifications

scenes.text: These models matter, and you should know their names, because you can comment on them and ask your own providers whether they participate. But no payment model makes a hand-off happen on its own. Someone still has to make the call, send the records, and follow up. Very often, that someone ends up being the care partner.

v.text: In a fragmented system, the person who follows up becomes the integrator. Too often that is an unpaid care partner. Course 3 is built to equip that person.

scenes.text: Your takeaway tool from this module is simple and powerful. Keep a one-page map of everyone involved in your care, with a name, a phone number, and the last thing they promised. When a hand-off fails, you will see exactly where, and you will know who to call.

v.title: The one-page care map
items: Every provider: name, role, direct phone
What each one last promised, and by when
Every referral: date sent, date received, outcome
Your insurer and plan type (traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage)

scenes.text: There's a saying in quality improvement: every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets. So let's look at the results, honestly, and then connect each one back to a design choice you've already seen.

v.sub: Every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets

scenes.prompt: Among people on dialysis in traditional Medicare, what share die in an average MONTH?
scenes.fb: About 2.0% per month from 2021 through 2024, up from about 1.6% in 2019 (MedPAC, March 2026). Roughly one person in fifty, every month.

scenes.text: About two percent a month. That sounds small until you do the arithmetic. One in fifty, every month, month after month. Before the pandemic it was about one point six percent. It rose in 2020 and has stayed near two percent since. In the same group, about fourteen to fifteen percent are admitted to the hospital in a given month, and about one in five hospital stays is followed by a readmission within thirty days.

items.label: visit an emergency department per month (2024)

v.src: MedPAC, March 2026 Report to the Congress, Ch. 5 (Medicare fee-for-service dialysis beneficiaries)

scenes.text: Home dialysis gives people more control over their time and often their health. It has grown. About eighteen percent of traditional Medicare dialysis patients dialyzed at home in 2024. But that still means more than eight in ten travel to a center, usually three times a week, for hours at a time, on a schedule set by someone else.

v.label: About 18 in 100 traditional Medicare dialysis patients dialyzed at home in 2024

scenes.text: Why hasn't home dialysis grown faster? Training requires nurses, and the largest provider has cited a challenging labor market as its main obstacle. Patients need space, supplies, and usually a trained partner at home. And for decades, the payment system and the clinic business model were built around in-center chairs. Medicare's ESRD Treatment Choices model, started in 2021, was designed to push the other way. The results so far are a slow climb, not a revolution.

v.title: Why home dialysis grows slowly
items: Space, supplies and a trained partner at home
A business model built around in-center chairs

scenes.text: Now look at who carries the burden. Compared with white Americans, Black Americans are more than four times as likely to develop kidney failure. Hispanic and Native American people are more than twice as likely. These gaps track the conditions we covered earlier, diabetes and high blood pressure, and they track access to the early care that prevents kidney failure.

v.title: Likelihood of developing kidney failure, compared with white Americans
v.src: NIDDK, citing USRDS 2023 Annual Data Report

scenes.text: And the gap continues into transplant. In 2024, Black patients made up about thirty-one percent of adults on the kidney waiting list, but only thirteen percent of people who received a kidney from a living donor. Living donation is the best option most patients have. Access to it depends heavily on who is around you and what resources they have. We'll go deep on this in Course 2.

scenes.prompt: Match each result to the design choice behind it. Tap to reveal.

cards.b: Payment for end-stage treatment, little for early detection (Module 1)
Negotiated private rates plus the 30-month coordination period (Module 3)

scenes.text: That is the machine. A promise made in 1972 that pays reliably at the end. A business model built on that promise, concentrated in two companies. A care system split into slices. And outcomes that fall hardest on the people with the least power to push back. In Course 2, we walk through the door that leads out of dialysis, transplant, and meet the gatekeepers who decide who gets through it.

quiz.q: Among traditional Medicare dialysis beneficiaries, about what share died per month from 2021 to 2024?

quiz.why: More than 4 times as likely (USRDS 2023, via NIDDK).

quiz.q: In 2024, Black patients were about 30.5% of the adult kidney waiting list. What share of living-donor kidney recipients were Black?
quiz.why: 13.0% (OPTN/SRTR 2024 Annual Data Report).

final.q: Which best describes the incentive built into the 1972 kidney failure entitlement?
o: Pay reliably for treatment after kidney failure
final.why: It paid for end-stage treatment and very little for keeping people from reaching it.

final.q: A patient has diabetes and falling filtration. What single addition to routine blood work most often catches early kidney damage?
final.why: Urine albumin detects damage that filtration alone can miss.

final.why: About a third of U.S. dialysis revenue (MedPAC, March 2026).

final.q: Which statement about the DaVita Justice Department settlements is accurate?
o: They resolved allegations without a determination of liability
final.why: Each resolved allegations; DOJ stated there was no determination of liability.

final.q: Two companies operate about what share of U.S. dialysis facilities?
final.why: About three quarters of 7,605 facilities (MedPAC, 2024 data).

What does the 30-month coordination period do?
o: Keeps an employer plan as primary payer before Medicare takes over
final.why: Private plans pay first for 30 months; this period is financially valuable to providers.

final.q: Which result best shows the human cost of late referral?
o: About 80% of hemodialysis starts through a catheter
final.why: Catheter starts track missing nephrology care: 93% with none versus 52% with a year or more.

final.q: What is the most useful first question when weighing a provider's recommendation, according to this course?
o: Under the payment rules, who gains if I say yes?
final.why: Seeing the incentive first helps you judge whose interest a recommendation serves.
